approachQuestion.prompt:
Order the Lab Ledger

A finite acyclic singly linked list stores integer keys in arbitrary order. Return the same nodes sorted by nondecreasing key, preserving original relative order for equal keys. Change only next links and preserve values. Access is by head and next, with no random access or bounded key range. Compare keys using comparisons only. Constraints: 0 <= n <= 200000.

Input: A(4) -> B(1) -> C(4) -> D(2). Output: B -> D -> A -> C -> null.
Input: null. Output: null.

Choose a method that satisfies the full contract with the best worst-case running time, breaking time ties by least auxiliary storage.

options.text: Recursively split the list into halves, stable-merge their sorted results iteratively, and return the sorted head.
options.feedback: This is correct and matches the comparison work, but the recursive splitting retains avoidable call frames.

options.text: Use the iterative run merges but take the right run first on equal keys.
options.feedback: For A(4) -> B(4), this can output B before A, violating stability.

options.text: Copy keys to an array, sort them, and write sorted keys into the original nodes without changing their order.
options.feedback: Node A(4) -> B(1) would become A(1) -> B(4); values must stay with their original nodes.

options.text: Count n, then iteratively merge adjacent runs of lengths 1, 2, 4 and so on. Cut each pair of runs, merge by head comparisons taking the left run on equality, append to the pass output, and repeat until the run width covers n.
options.feedback: Each pass combines stable sorted runs; taking from the left on equality preserves original equal-key order.

feedback.reason: Each pass combines stable sorted runs; taking from the left on equality preserves original equal-key order.
details: Count n, then iteratively merge adjacent runs of lengths 1, 2, 4 and so on. Cut each pair of runs, merge by head comparisons taking the left run on equality, append to the pass output, and repeat until the run width covers n.

Bottom-up run widths double after each pass, avoiding a recursive call stack. Taking the left equal key preserves stable ordering. Cut run boundaries before merging so the merge cannot escape into unprocessed nodes.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the revealed method (acm-b15-13-target), regardless of your Q1 choice. Here n is the input node count; write log(n+1) so the expression covers empty and singleton lists. Choose the tight worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Count each node allocation, link access, identity/value comparison and machine-word operation as constant work. Include all temporary collections and call frames; exclude supplied nodes and the final returned output only. Copying or allocating k records costs k operations. No hash-table, amortized-operation or tail-call assumptions are used.

options.explanation: This pair does not describe the fixed method. Each merge pass scans at most n nodes and run width doubles, giving logarithmically many passes. Arbitrarily interleaved keys force linear merging work per pass for large n. Counting costs linear time. Cutting and iterative merging retain fixed references and counters, with no recursion or node-reference array.
